name: The Break: How 2022-2024 Shattered the Commodity Contract
deck: Iran sanctions, DRC cobalt quotas, and Middle East energy disruptions between 2021-2023 broke the contract that had stabilized commodity flows for 30 years. Now every link in the supply chain passes volatility forward immediately instead of absorbing it, moving the pain from producers to consumers and small operators with no hedging tools.
core_bet: A structural break occurred between 2021 and 2023. The post-Cold War inventory-buffering, long-term-contracting system that had smoothed commodity cost swings for three decades fractured under geopolitical stress. Iran's removal from phosphate markets, DRC's cobalt quota system, and Middle East energy disruptions were not temporary shocks—they were permanent policy shifts that destroyed the assumptions underlying the prior contract. Every commodity producer learned that holding inventory or absorbing a price swing was economically worse than passing costs forward immediately. The inventories that once smoothed shocks were drained. Long-term contracts were renegotiated at higher prices or not renewed at all. The default mode shifted from 'absorb and recover' to 'pass through immediately.'

mechanism: The pre-2022 contract worked because geopolitical risk seemed manageable. Russia supplied Europe; Iran supplied phosphate markets under sanctions but not at crisis levels; Africa's mines exported consistently; China controlled rare earths but within negotiated bounds. Under that stability, commodity companies signed long-term contracts, built inventory buffers, and planned for gradual cost pass-through over quarters or years. A fertilizer producer like CF Industries would contract ammonia supplies multi-year, maintain strategic reserves, and absorb short-term cost swings knowing they would recover over time. Glencore used its dual industrial-and-trading structure to hold inventory and trade optionally when spreads widened. Mosaic planned phosphate rock and ammonia sourcing with confidence that supply and prices would stabilize within predictable ranges. This structure required patience, capital tied up in inventory, and willingness to sacrifice quarterly margin to preserve customer relationships and supply continuity.

The 2021-2023 period broke every assumption. Iran sanctions tightened, cutting phosphate sources permanently off global markets. DRC implemented cobalt quota regimes that prioritized extraction over processing, forcing Glencore and other miners to hold unprocessed ore as inventory—asset on the balance sheet, not tradeable commodity. Middle East conflicts spiked energy costs and stopped supply flows, raising petrochemical and fertilizer production costs. These were not cyclical disruptions; they were policy ruptures that created structural scarcity. Inventory buffers that were built for smoothing 10-15% price swings proved inadequate for 30-40% swings driven by geopolitical fracture. Long-term contracts were exposed as liabilities when prices moved beyond contract ranges. Customer relationships that relied on price stability became irrelevant when supply tightened.

The response was immediate pass-through. CF Industries shifted from contract stability to dynamic pricing: pass ammonia and nitrogen costs directly to customers and use cash flow for buybacks and dividends rather than building reserves. Glencore's marketing business (trading adjusted EBIT of $2.9B in 2025) became the profit center precisely because supply disruption created trading opportunities—the company could monetize scarcity rather than manage through it by buying low and selling high when disruption tightened supply. Mosaic faced the harshest truth: sulfur became a binding constraint with contract prices swinging from $440/ton to $705/ton across quarters. The company had no buffering options; it could only pass costs forward, curtail production when margins turned negative, and accept working-capital destruction from inventory and pricing volatility. By H1 2026, Glencore's cobalt production had fallen 46% not because demand collapsed but because the DRC quota forced miners to choose: either export at quota-constrained rates or hold inventory and wait. Producers chose to pass the problem forward and let customers deal with the scarcity.
why_now: The 2021-2023 fracture is structural, not cyclical, and it is not reversing. Cold War ended with a period of relative geopolitical consensus on commodity supply: Middle East oil flowed consistently, African mines operated under stable regimes, Russia was integrated into European energy markets, and long-term contracting was possible because political risk seemed manageable. That era ended sharply between 2021 and 2023. Iran sanctions escalated, cutting off phosphate permanently. Russian energy was weaponized and integrated into Western Europe no longer. DRC implemented quota regimes that are policy decisions, not temporary shortages. China's rare-earth restrictions tightened. The inventory buffers built during the prior era were drained during COVID. Long-term contracts are being renegotiated at much higher base prices or simply not renewed. Each link in the supply chain has learned that absorbing a cost spike is economically worse than passing it forward immediately. CF's guidance for 2026 (9.5M tons ammonia, down from 2025's 10.1M) shows not temporary disruption but capacity withdrawal. The new normal is: hold less inventory, accept higher volatility, pass costs forward instantly.
who_pays: Farmers buying nitrogen fertilizer now face CF's full pass-through of ammonia costs plus company margins, with no contractual protection. Battery makers buying cobalt face Glencore's spot pricing instead of the contract rates that used to buffer supply shocks. Plastic manufacturers buying polymers face Middle East energy shocks, petrochemical spreads, and raw-material volatility without any contractual cushion. Small businesses and farmers without hedging capability face margin compression and inability to invest. Consumers face higher food prices when fertilizer costs spike because there is no buffer in the supply chain to absorb the swing. The transfer mechanism is simple: each link passes the pain forward to whoever has the least bargaining power.
who_profits: Commodity producers positioned at the source of scarcity. CF Industries captured $1.46B of net income in FY 2025 despite a constrained global ammonia market because it owns production assets and can pass through all costs instantly. Glencore's marketing business earned $2.9B in adjusted EBIT in 2025 precisely because supply disruption creates profit opportunities for traders who can monetize scarcity spreads. LyondellBasell benefits from its North American feedstock advantage when Middle East energy costs spike—it produces cheaper and captures the spread. The ultimate winners are whoever sits at the chokepoint: a cobalt miner under DRC quota, a natural-gas producer feeding ammonia plants, a broker matching sulfur buyers to available inventory. The next level of winners: companies integrated backward into commodity inputs (like integrated petrochemical producers) escape the pass-through and capture the spread themselves.
tension: This model breaks if geopolitical risk reverses or demand destruction forces a reset. If Iran reintegrates into global trade, phosphate supplies surge and prices collapse, invalidating the pass-through-immediately strategy. If cobalt demand falls faster than DRC's quota regime persists, miners are left with inventory at declining prices. If energy prices collapse due to LNG surge or energy transition acceleration, petrochemical margins compress and trading profit evaporates. The deeper tension is customer push-back: if enough farmers, battery makers, or end-users integrate backward or find substitutes, they break the pricing power that pass-through depends on. A battery maker might shift to lower-cobalt chemistries; a farmer might switch crops or consolidate. The last tension is regulatory: if enough governments recognize commodity-price volatility's impact on food security or energy transitions, they may impose price controls or long-term contracting requirements that reverse the shift backward toward buffering.
surprising_part: The insight that is hardest to see is that commodity-price volatility is now a profit center, not a cost center. CF Industries, Glencore, and other commodity producers are not trying to reduce price swings anymore; they are trying to capture the spread of that volatility. Glencore explicitly defends its marketing business and calls it a profit engine during disruption. CF uses strong cash generation to fund buybacks rather than build inventory buffers. They have learned that volatility is profitable for those with balance-sheet strength to absorb it, and that passing through costs immediately locks in that profit. The old model—absorb the shock, smooth the customer relationship, recover over time—is gone because geopolitical shocks are now permanent features, not temporary cycles. That is the real inflection: the risk model inverted.
one_sentence: Post-2022 geopolitical fragmentation broke the long-term contract and inventory-buffer system—commodity companies shifted from shock absorbers to shock transmitters that pass all pain forward immediately.
societal_stake: This shift cascades into food prices, energy costs, and industrial investment. When fertilizer costs spike and are passed through immediately, food prices rise faster and small farmers cannot absorb the shock. When energy costs spike and are passed through immediately, petrochemical and manufacturing costs rise, rippling into packaging, mobility, and construction. The buffer that used to exist—allowing time for adjustment, contracting, and gradual pass-through—is gone. Supply shocks now hit end consumers and small producers within quarters rather than years, creating more turbulent demand, higher volatility in sectors that feed real people, and faster wage pressure in food and energy-dependent economies.
